name: Oruma
confidence_why: Kay Williamson, the fieldworker on Ijo, classes Oruma as a two-tone language both in her 1988 study of Ijo tone and accent (dialect 11 OR, a two-level tone system without downstep) and in her 1994 encyclopedia article, and no source reports word stress for it; the record rests on one author's fieldwork, and her two accounts differ only on whether the system has downstep, a detail that does not touch the type.

catalog_quote: [Williamson 2009 [1994], pp. 517-518, open] West Ijọ consists first of the inland Ijọ group, comprising three isolated languages: Biseni, Akita (Okordia), and Tugbeni (Oruma); and second of Izon, a large language with a complex dialect situation. ... Typically, Ijọ dialects have vowel harmony with nine oral and nine nasal vowels, though some have reduced the number. Labio velar stops occur in all dialects; in many dialects they are in contrast with voiced implosives. KAKIBA and inland Ijọ have two tones plus downstep, some Izon dialects have two tones without downstep, while many other Izon dialects and Nembe-Akaha have pitch-accent systems. The typical root structure is CVCV(CV) (where C = Consonant and V = Vowel). || [Williamson 1988, pp. 253, 254, 276-277, archive.org full-text-search fragments:] In terms of the usual typology, dialects 11-12, 312-319 would be classified as two-levei tone systems without downstep, dialects 13-311 as two-level tone systems with downstep, and dialects 321-42 as pitch-accent systems. These different characterizations of otherwise closely-related, often mutually intelligible, dialects raise doubts as to the usefulness of this typology. ... The dialect names are abbreviated as follows: OR = Oruma GB = Gbanrain ... 11 OR HH HH HL HH

new_statements.rule_in_words: Oruma (Williamson's dialect 11, Inland Ijo cluster) is a two-level (H/L) tone language without downstep; lexical morpheme classes surface in isolation as e.g. Class A HH/HH, Class B HL/HH. As in all Ijo lects, surface pitch is computed over syntactically defined groups whose pattern is determined by the class of the group-initial morpheme ('first morpheme strong, others weak'). Nothing is said about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Williamson notes that in Table 1 an initial V-syllable sometimes behaves differently from an initial CV-syllable; Williamson & Blench 2006 (ELL2) instead generalise 'inland Ijo' (Biseni, Okordia, Oruma) as 'two tones plus downstep', whereas the 1988 table has Oruma without downstep and Okordia with downstep.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone classes of morphemes in isolation (citation forms) and the phonological 'group' (object+verb, noun+modifiers) as the domain of pitch realisation; group-initial morpheme prominence is a phrase-level tonal dominance fact, not word stress. Text was read as verbatim scanned served by archive.org full-text search of the lending scan (scan itself not downloadable); excerpts with provenance saved in the file named.
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 1988 treats Oruma as dialect '11 OR' of the Inland Ijo cluster (cluster 1: Oruma, Biseni, Okordia) within the Ijo dialect continuum; Williamson & Blench 2006 call it 'Tugbeni (Oruma)', one of three 'isolated languages' of inland Ijo. Same variety as Glottolog orum1241 / ISO orr (Oruma town and Ibelebiri, Ogbia LGA, Bayelsa; an enclave within Ogbia-speaking territory). The ELL2 generalisation ('inland Ijo.. two tones plus downstep') covers Biseni (bise1238) and Okordia (okod1238) as well and differs from the 1988 table, which shows Oruma without downstep.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement (Williamson 1988): Oruma is a two-tone language with no stress statement; the catalog record itself has an empty rule. One detail differs: Williamson 1988 (sec. 1.1, Table 1 row '11 OR') classes Oruma among the 'two-level tone systems without downstep', whereas this 1994 encyclopedia article says 'inland Ijo' (Biseni, Okordia, Oruma together) has 'two tones plus downstep' -- a generalisation over the three inland lects that fits Okordia (1988 dialect 13, with downstep) but not the 1988 placement of Oruma. Byline is 'K Williamson, University of Port Harcourt', (c) 1994 Elsevier -- single author, not Williamson & Blench; the ELL2 2006 printing carries the 1…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article treats the whole Ijo cluster; Oruma (Tugbeni) is placed in the 'inland Ijo' group, which is characterised as having two lexical tones plus downstep. Nothing is said about word stress, accent placement or prominence; the word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the article (checked on both the PDF text and the scanned).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the tone characterisation is stated at the level of the inland Ijo group (Biseni, Okordia, Oruma), not for Oruma individually
new_statements.identity_note: The 1994/2009 article describes the Ijo cluster as a whole; Oruma appears only as 'Tugbeni (Oruma)', one of the three isolated inland Ijo languages (with Biseni and Akita/Okordia), and the tone characterisation is given for 'inland Ijo' collectively. Williamson 1988 (existing statement) uses the dialect code 11 OR = Oruma directly.

readall_conflicts: One internal disagreement between Kay Williamson's own two descriptions on a tone detail, not on stress: Williamson 1988 (Tone and accent in Ijo, sec. 1.1 p. 253 and Table 1 p. 254, dialect 11 = OR = Oruma) puts Oruma among the 'two-level tone systems without downstep', while her 1994 ELL article (repr. 2009, p. 518) states that 'inland Ijo' as a group (Biseni, Okordia, Oruma) has 'two tones plus downstep'. The 1994 statement is a group-level generalisation and does not name Oruma individually; the 1988 Table gives Oruma's own isolation patterns (Class A HH/HH, Class B HL/HH) with no downstep mark, and gives Okordia (13 OA) H'H with downstep. On the point that matters for the catalog -- a tone language with no word-stress statement -- the two sources agree.
